title: Coach Carter
full_review:
When a basketball coach at a Richmond, Calif., high school, grounded his team after the players failed to maintain basic academic standards, he made headlines in early 1999. That story now comes to the screen in the formulaic but interesting "Coach Carter" (Paramount).

Ken Carter (Samuel L. Jackson) accepts a job at the high school with the stipulation that the players sign contracts agreeing to achieve decent grades and sit in the front row of their classes.

The team is a tough bunch, but Carter shows right from the start who's boss, and doles out penalties -- namely, hundreds of push-ups or "suicides" (running back and forth) -- at the sign of any resistance or sassing.

Though many on the team seem like bad news, underneath it all, we're made to see they're really good kids, even the tough-talking Timo Cruz (Rick Gonzalez), who tells Carter off on his first day, but then comes back penitently when he misses the camaraderie on the team. The Cruz story is admirable in its depiction of a young man torn between the easy life of drug dealing and walking the straighter path of his teammates.

Carter's son, Damien (Robert Ri'chard), joins the team, after imploring his father to transfer him from the private school he's attending so he can play basketball, but Carter insists he maintain an even higher average than the other boys.

Then there's Kenyon Stone (Rob Brown), who's gotten girlfriend Kyra (played by singer Ashanti in her big screen debut) pregnant, but has every intention of doing right by her. But after they temporarily split, Kyra indeed has an abortion, which Kenyon learns when he comes back ready to make a life with her and the baby. The film has already established these kids would be over their heads with a child. Still, there's the unfortunate moral that, under the circumstances, she did the "right thing." Kyra tells him, "I had a choice to make, so I made it. For me." Kenyon is saddened, but chastising her for her action he merely expresses regret that he wasn't around to support her.

When Carter learns that the boys are doing poorly in their studies -- and he finds out relatively late in the game, as the teachers were reluctant to provide him with the requested progress reports, thinking his methods too unorthodox -- he immediately suspends the basketball games and padlocks the gym, much to the consternation of the principal with whom he's been at polite loggerheads from the start (Denise Dowse).

The parents are up in arms because -- apart from pride in the local team -- they view the game as the only activity keeping many of their kids in school and as their only chance of advancement. Carter, himself a Richmond High graduate, is aware of the dismal success rate of kids from that school going to college, and holds firm to his conviction of the kids deserving a better life.

Mark Schwahn and John Gatins' script is good, even as it recycles themes which, in their essentials, we've seen before.

The film directed by Thomas Carter (no relation) is reasonably absorbing, and Jackson gives a compellingly tough and unsentimental performance. Though some parents may feel it's important for inner-city kids to see this inspiring story with its message extolling academic achievement and teamwork, be warned that there's a good deal of crude language (unfortunately true to life), and the aforementioned abortion subplot with its questionable moral implications, which preclude the film from getting the A-II rating its subject matter would seem to imply.

The film contains much crude language, drug dealing, some violence, abortion, suggestive dancing and sexual situations. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
